title: Santa Claus Conquers the Martians

evidence.note: Renewal absence cannot make this 1964 film public domain. For a work first published in 1964, 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) says a renewal application 'is not a condition of the renewal and extension of the copyright', so the renewal term attaches automatically. Public domain would have to rest on a missing copyright notice on the 1964 release prints, and I could not verify that from any source I fetched. Plagiarism Today and Wikipedia say the film is public domain in the US but do not document the basis.
Sound film. The recorded soundtrack normally shares the film's status, so it is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I did not verify any separate music copyright or registration.
I did not confirm the source of the story or whether it was published or registered separately from the film, so the story layer is undetermined.

Plagiarism Today says that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds the copyright and enforces it. I did not confirm any specific restoration or its added material. Any cleaned-up transfer, new titles or added commentary would be protectable even if the underlying print were free.

editorial:
Santa Claus Conquers the Martians is a 1964 children's science-fiction comedy directed by Nicholas Webster, with John Call as Santa Claus. Martian leaders fear their children have gone lazy and joyless from watching Earth TV, so they abduct Santa. It was made on a roughly $200,000 budget in about two weeks in July and August 1964 at Michael Myerberg Studios on Long Island. It later became a cult title and was featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000 in 1991.

The rights trap is the usual shortcut that an old film was never renewed. A film published in 1964 got its renewal term automatically under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so renewal is not what decides this one. It would have to be free for another reason, such as a missing notice, and I found no document establishing that. Secondary sources call it public domain in the US only, and Plagiarism Today says STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces rights abroad. Check the notice on an actual print before reusing it, and keep it out of non-US distribution.
faq: Is Santa Claus Conquers the Martians public domain because the copyright was not renewed?

That reason does not work for a 1964 film. Under 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) a renewal application is not a condition of the renewal term, so the term attaches automatically. The film could be public domain in the US only through a defect such as a missing copyright notice. I could not verify one, so the status is undetermined here.
Can I use the Internet Archive copy, including outside the US?

The Internet Archive copy is a community upload, and I have not verified its source or quality beyond its metadata. Plagiarism Today reports that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces the copyright. For anything beyond US use, get a clearance first.
